results.title: DISC Test Results Explained: Reading Your Chart and Profile
results.description: How to read your DISC test results: the three chart lines, percentages, primary and secondary styles and a balanced profile, plus examples and common mistakes.
results.lead: A DISC test result is more than a single letter. It’s a chart with three lines, percentages for the four styles and a profile of one or two letters. Below, we use examples to walk through what each part of the report means and how to avoid misreading it.

p: After the last block, you see four things: your profile name with one or two letters (for example, “Pioneer, DI”), a chart with three lines, four scales with percentages and a written description. The description covers your traits, strengths, growth areas, motivation, behavior under stress and tips on how others can best communicate with you. You can also save the same report as a PDF and reopen it from its link.

Every number in the report comes from your marks in the 24 blocks. In each block, you chose one statement as “most like me” and one as “least like me,” and each statement belongs to one of the styles: D, I, S or C. So each style has two numbers: how many times you picked it as “most” and how many times as “least.”

sections.h: The three lines on the chart
p: The overall profile (the bold line with colored dots) is the main one. It’s the difference between your “most” and “least” marks for each style, converted to a scale from 0 to 24. The midline of the scale is 12, shown as a dashed line on the chart. A style above the midline counts as high; one below it counts as low.

The adapted style is the line built from your “most” marks. It shows how you try to behave at work, the image you consciously keep up. The natural style is the line built from your “least” marks, inverted: the less often you rejected a style, the higher its point. It’s closer to how you act on autopilot, without effort: under pressure, for example, or in an unfamiliar situation.

If all three lines track each other, you behave much the same in any setting. If your adapted and natural styles pull apart, treat it as a clue rather than a problem: you’re switching on a style by sheer willpower. Most often, that means your role calls for behavior that doesn’t come naturally to you, and that behavior costs you energy.

Your primary style is the one with the highest overall score. It’s the first letter of your profile and the basis of the description. A secondary style counts if its score is positive and at least 40% of the primary one (with a minimum of 3 points on the “raw” scale from −24 to +24). It becomes the second letter and adds a shade to the description: a D with a secondary I (DI) persuades with drive and enthusiasm, a D with a secondary C (DC) with firm demands and solid arguments.

The order of the letters matters: DI and ID are different profiles. In DI, Dominance leads and Influence backs it up. In ID, the person is sociable and inspiring first and turns on the pressure when needed. If the second style’s score is negative or well below the primary one, the profile stays “pure”: D, I, S or C.

The percentages on the four scales are the same overall score converted to a scale from 0 to 100: −24 equals 0%, 0 equals 50% and +24 equals 100%. Above 50% means you chose the style more often than you rejected it; below 50% means the reverse. The number doesn’t tell you “how much D is in me.” It measures how typical the style is for you compared with the other three.

The “raw” scores of the four styles always add up to zero, because the test compares the styles with one another rather than measuring each on its own. So a high score in one style inevitably means a low score in another. The opposites are usually D and S or I and C, which sit at opposite ends of the pace and focus axes.

If no score rises clearly above the midline, the report calls the profile balanced but still names a primary style based on the highest number. A result like this most often means flexibility: you switch between styles as the situation demands, and colleagues of every style find you equally easy to work with.

Less often, a flat chart means you answered hesitantly, overthought your answers or tried to pick the “right” ones. It’s easy to check: take the test again in a few days, answering quickly with a specific work role in mind. If the profile is flat again, flexibility really is your defining trait.

sections.h: What to do with your result
p: Start with the description of your strengths and growth areas: note what you recognize and what seems off. Then read the “How others can best communicate with you” section and ask yourself whether your colleagues know this. The most useful thing you can do with a result is talk about it. Compare profiles with your team on the style compatibility page and agree on how to work with your differences.

A profile is neither a verdict nor a ceiling. It describes how you usually behave now, and it may shift with a new role, experience and circumstances. It’s worth saving the link to your report and retaking the test in a year. The changes will show how your work has shaped you.

sections.h: Common mistakes in reading your result
ul: Treating one style as “the best.” Every style has strengths and a cost: D’s drive turns into impatience, C’s thoroughness into missed deadlines.
Mixing up the order of the letters. DI and ID, SC and CS are different profiles with different primary styles.
Reading the percentages as shares. A 70% in D doesn’t mean “70% dominant.” It means you chose the D style noticeably more often than you rejected it.
Drawing conclusions about competence. DISC describes behavioral style, not ability, intelligence or fitness for a job.
Judging others by their results. The report is a self-assessment, and the person knows best where the description fits and where it misses.

examples.text: The overall profile is high in D and I and low in S and C. The primary style is Dominance (D). Influence (I) is also high and counts as secondary, so the profile is DI, “Pioneer.” This person makes decisions fast and brings people along, but often has little patience for details and too little caution.

The mirror image: S and C above the midline, D and I below it. The primary style is Steadiness (S) and the secondary one is Conscientiousness (C), so the profile is SC, “Specialist.” This person is methodical, reliable and follows the rules, but sudden change and pressure are hard on them.

All four scores are close to the midline. A primary style is technically assigned by the highest number, but the report notes that the profile is balanced. Most likely, this person adapts their style to the situation. If the answers were hesitant, it’s worth taking the test again.

colors.title: DISC Colors: Red, Yellow, Green and Blue Personality Types
colors.description: Red, yellow, green and blue DISC personality types: how to spot each color, how to work with it and where Surrounded by Idiots fits in. Free test.
colors.h1: DISC colors: red, yellow, green, blue
colors.lead: The four DISC styles are often labeled with colors: red for Dominance, yellow for Influence, green for Steadiness and blue for Conscientiousness. The colors don’t add anything to the model, but they make the styles easy to remember and to talk about as a team. Here’s what each color stands for and how to find yours.

D.name: Red
D.text: Red is the color of speed and drive. “Reds” set a goal and head straight for it. They decide fast, argue, take responsibility and don’t shy away from conflict. On a team they push the work forward, but they can come on too strong and lose patience with people who work more carefully.
signs: Keeps it brief and gets straight to the bottom line.
Decides fast and doesn’t like decisions being put off.
Speaks up in meetings, argues and sets the pace.
Sends two-line messages with no greeting and no emoji.
Under pressure, gets curt and starts making every call alone.
D.blind: “Reds” shine at getting things moving while everyone else is still talking. The blind spot is what that pace costs: they don’t notice that people haven’t had time to get on board, and they read caution as weakness and questions as pushback. What annoys them most is slowness, empty talk and losing control.
talk: Lead with the goal and the conclusion; save the details for when they ask.
Offer options rather than one solution. They want to make the call themselves.
Disagree directly and bring facts. Hints and sulking don’t register with them.

I.name: Yellow
I.text: Yellow is the color of energy and connection. “Yellows” make friends easily, inspire others, come up with ideas and spread optimism. They value recognition and genuine personal connection. Details, deadlines and routine are harder for them, and their promises sometimes run ahead of what’s possible.
signs: Strikes up conversations with strangers and is on a first-name basis in no time.
Tells stories, gestures a lot, and their mood is contagious.
Comes up with ideas on the fly and is the first to volunteer.
Writes with flair: exclamation points, emoji, voice messages.
Under pressure, talks a lot, overpromises and looks for support.
I.blind: “Yellows” shine at bringing people together and firing them up about an idea. The blind spot is follow-through: their interest fades once the routine starts, deadlines and details slide, and they promise more than they can deliver. What hurts them most is indifference, being criticized in front of others and working alone.
talk: Start with a personal connection: a few words about them, then get down to business.
Praise them visibly and sincerely. Recognition motivates them more than anything.
Put agreements in writing, with dates, or they may forget them.

S.name: Green
S.text: Green is the color of calm and reliability. “Greens” listen well, support others, finish what they start and look after relationships on the team. They need predictability and time to adjust to change, and they find open conflict and pressure hard to handle.
signs: Listens more than they talk and asks how you’re doing.
Doesn’t rush to answer and takes time to think things over.
Is glad to help and rarely says no, even when overloaded.
Sticks to the familiar: the same route, the same tools, the same team.
Under pressure, goes quiet, agrees on the surface and lets resentment build.
S.blind: “Greens” are the reliable ones: they see things through and keep relationships intact where others would end up at odds. The blind spot is silence. They don’t say no, don’t argue openly and go along with changes they privately disagree with. What throws them off most is sudden change, a harsh tone and conflict.
talk: Tell them about changes ahead of time and explain why they’re needed.
Ask for their opinion one-on-one, not in the middle of a group debate.
Don’t take silence for agreement. Check what they really think.

C.name: Blue
C.text: Blue is the color of analysis and order. “Blues” rely on facts, check the details, plan ahead and follow standards. They’re the ones who keep quality up, but they can get stuck in analysis, let deadlines slip while chasing perfection and come across as cold.
signs: Asks follow-up questions and wants numbers, sources and examples.
Gathers information and compares options before deciding.
Spots errors, typos and inconsistencies that others miss.
Writes in detail, in bullet points, with attachments and links.
Under pressure, retreats into analysis, puts off decisions and turns critical.
C.blind: “Blues” stand for quality: their work rarely has to be redone. The blind spot is the cost of perfection: they spend time checking work that’s already good enough, hold off on decisions until everything is clear and sound cold when someone needs support. What irritates them most is sloppiness, rushing for no reason and vague wording.
talk: Come with facts and structure: goal, data, options, deadlines.
Give them time to review the material before the meeting, not during it.
Keep criticism specific: what exactly is wrong and by what standard.

p: William Marston, who created the four-factor model, didn’t use colors. He called his four dimensions Dominance, Inducement, Submission and Compliance. The colors came later, when trainers started teaching the model in workshops. Four colors are easier to remember than four letters, and they work well on posters, on cards and in group discussions.

There’s no single standard, but the most common scheme is the one this site uses: red D, yellow I, green S, blue C. The logic is simple. The “warm” colors go to the fast, assertive styles and the “cool” ones to the more measured styles. Some systems swap yellow and green, so when you compare results from different sources, go by the letters, not the colors.

sections.h: Two axes instead of four colors
p: The colors make more sense once you see the two axes behind them. The first is pace: red and yellow act quickly and decisively, green and blue deliberately and carefully. The second is focus: red and blue concentrate on tasks and results, yellow and green on people and relationships. Each color is simply a point where the two axes meet, not a separate “breed” of people.

That’s why neighboring colors resemble each other and opposite colors differ the most: red and green (D and S), yellow and blue (I and C). These are the pairs that misunderstand each other most often on a team, and they’re also the ones that complement each other best once they’ve agreed on ground rules.

Pure colors are rare. Most people have two strong styles, a primary and a secondary one, so a test result usually looks like “red with yellow” (the DI profile) or “green with blue” (SC). Instead of simply assigning you a color, the test on this site shows how strong all four styles are, in percent and on a chart.

You can also make a rough guess without the test. If you decide quickly and push for results, you’re probably red. If you make friends easily and energize people, yellow. If you’re patient, reliable and avoid conflict, green. If you check every detail and dislike being rushed, blue. But eyeballing it often gives a different answer than the test, because people tend to see themselves in whatever style their environment values.

sections.h: Color tests and DISC: what’s the difference?
p: Some typologies are built around colors in their own right. The best known is Insights Discovery, which uses the same red, yellow, green and blue. These systems grew out of Jung’s work and differ from DISC in the details: different questions, a different scale, a different reading of the nuances. Similar color names don’t mean you’ll get the same result.

Then there are popular “what color are you?” quizzes with a dozen or so questions. They’re fun, but they don’t separate a primary style from a secondary one, don’t show how strong each style is and don’t tell you what to do with the result. The 24-block DISC test gives you all of that, and it’s still free.

sections.h: The colors in Thomas Erikson’s Surrounded by Idiots
p: Most people know the four colors mainly from Surrounded by Idiots, a book by the Swedish author Thomas Erikson (original title Omgiven av idioter, 2014). It has sold millions of copies and has been translated into dozens of languages. Erikson describes the same four characters as DISC: the decisive, impatient red; the sociable, enthusiastic yellow; the calm, accommodating green; and the precise, reserved blue. The title is ironic: people of a different color seem like idiots to us until we understand what makes them tick.

Erikson builds directly on DISC, so his red, yellow, green and blue match the D, I, S and C styles on this site. Where they differ is the approach: the book explains the model through everyday stories and familiar characters, while the test measures how strong each style is. In Sweden, psychologists and the skeptics’ association Vetenskap och Folkbildning criticized the book for oversimplifying and for presenting a popular read as if it were backed by science. That’s a fair warning for any color scheme: use it as a shared language for conversation, not as a diagnosis.

Mapping your team by color is a quick way to spot imbalances. A team made up entirely of “reds” makes decisions fast and clashes just as fast. A team of “greens” gets along well but avoids hard conversations and puts off change. A mixed team works better when everyone knows what to expect from the other colors: how to hand off a task, how to give feedback, how to disagree.

The style compatibility page covers every pair: what they have in common, where friction comes from and what each person can do about it. For managers and HR, there’s a separate guide to running the test with a team and talking through the results.

A color is a label, and labels oversimplify. “Well, you’re a red” sounds like an excuse for rudeness, and “they’re green, what do you expect?” sounds like you’ve stopped expecting anything from them. DISC describes habitual behavior. Character, values and abilities are outside its scope, and any style can be developed. Use the colors to understand each other, not to put people in boxes.

sections.h: When you need a paper version
p: A paper test comes in handy at a training session or strategy offsite where not everyone has a computer, in a classroom and anywhere phones aren’t allowed. Some people just focus better on paper: you mark an answer, turn the page, and no notifications get in the way.

If participants do have their phones, the online version is simpler. It scores the result, draws the chart, saves the report as a PDF and gives you a link to share. For teams, there’s also an admin panel that collects everyone’s results.

sections.h: How to fill out and score the test
p: In each block, mark the one statement that describes you most and the one that describes you least. Answer based on how you usually act at work, and don’t overthink it. Then use the key to write the style letter next to each mark and count the “most like me” and “least like me” marks for each style.

Subtract the second count from the first to get the style’s total, from −24 to +24. The style with the highest total is primary. If the second-highest total is positive and at least 40% of the primary one (and no less than 3), that’s the secondary style. The result is a one- or two-letter profile, such as D or DI. Its description is in the file, and a detailed explanation with examples is on a separate page.

sections.h: A report for your paper result
p: The paper version gives you a profile and a short description. For the summary report with the chart, strengths, growth areas and communication tips, open your profile’s page from the list of 16 profiles or take the test online. It takes about 10 minutes.

teams.title: DISC Assessment for Teams and HR: How to Use It at Work
teams.description: How to use DISC with a team: style map, roles, conflict, onboarding, feedback and sales. Run the free test with your whole team and talk through the results.
teams.lead: Most people take DISC with their team, not on their own. Teams use it to understand why colleagues react differently, agree on how they’ll communicate and assign roles sensibly. This page shows how a manager or HR can run the test, read the team map and discuss the results without labeling anyone.

p: Most friction at work comes down to style rather than competence. One person wants to decide quickly, another wants to check first; one speaks bluntly, another finds bluntness rude. DISC gives you a shared language for these differences. Instead of “they’re impossible,” you hear “they’re a high D, they need short answers and results.” The differences don’t go away, but people stop taking them as personal dislike.

The second benefit is clear expectations. When everyone’s report spells out how others can best communicate with them, the manager doesn’t have to guess who needs freedom, who needs clear criteria, who should hear about changes early and who should be thanked in public.

sections.h: The team map: what the mix of styles shows
p: Gather everyone’s profiles and look at the proportions. A D-heavy team decides fast and takes risks, but often clashes and tunes out the cautious voices. An I-heavy team brings energy and ideas, but deadlines and details suffer. An S-heavy team is close-knit and reliable, but avoids hard conversations and puts off change. A C-heavy team keeps quality high, but decisions drag on and anything new meets skepticism.

Gaps matter more than imbalances. With no high C on the team, nobody checks the work or plans for risks; with no I, nobody sells ideas outside the team or keeps spirits up. That isn’t a reason to hire for the “missing type.” It’s a reason to fill the gap on purpose: make someone responsible for checking or for communication, and give them time for it.

ul: A conflict between two colleagues. It’s usually a pair of opposite styles: D and S, or I and C. Look up the pair on the compatibility page and suggest one specific change in how each of them communicates.
A new hire. A test taken during onboarding tells the mentor how to bring the person up to speed: an S needs clear rules and time, a D needs a task of their own from day one.

Assigning roles on a project. Launches and negotiations go to people high in D and I; support and quality, to people high in S and C. Treat this as a guide, not a restriction. People can handle work outside their comfort zone; it just takes more energy.
Feedback. A C needs facts and time to think, an I needs their contribution recognized before any criticism, an S needs a calm one-on-one, and a D needs it short and to the point, with no preamble.

Sales and negotiations. Read the client’s style from how they behave and speak their language: results and deadlines for a D, relationships and emotions for an I, guarantees and reliability for an S, data and comparisons for a C.

sections.h: How to run the test with your team on this site
ol: Take the test yourself. You’ll know what participants will see, and you can show them a sample report.

Send your colleagues a link to the site in the language they need. No sign-up is required, and the test takes about 10 minutes. The report shows up on screen right away; each person can save it as a PDF and forward you the link to their result.
Ask each person to send you the link to their result or the code from their report. Only people with the link can see a result, and nothing is sent to the manager automatically.

Open the admin panel (linked in the site footer) and paste in the codes you’ve received. The panel builds a table with names, profiles and scores that you can copy into Excel. The table is stored only in your browser.
Set up a team meeting: explain the four styles, show the team map and let everyone say what in their report rang true and what didn’t.

p: Rule one: the result belongs to the participant. Nobody has to show their report, and the discussion starts with each person talking about themselves. Rule two: there are no good or bad styles. Whenever someone says “D is better for a manager,” remind them that every style has its costs and that a team needs all four.

One format that works: each person makes a request by finishing two sentences, “It helps me when…” and “It gets in my way when…” Said out loud and written down, these sentences do more for a team than any typology. Come back to them in two or three months and see what has changed.

In an interview, DISC works as a starting point for talking about work style and as a hint about what to ask: for example, how a high-C candidate handles uncertainty. But don’t base a hiring decision on a profile. The method describes behavioral preferences, not competence, motivation, experience or fit for the job, and any style can succeed in almost any role.

A note on ethics: ask a candidate to take the test only after you explain why and who will see the result. The test isn’t a diagnostic tool, and using it to screen people out means losing good candidates and putting your reputation at risk.

ul: Labeling people. “You’re an S, you won’t mind anyway” turns a tool for understanding into an excuse for neglect.
Expecting everyone in a department to have the same profile. Teams where everyone is alike are blind to what they can’t do.
Running the test without discussing it. A report nobody talks about is forgotten within a week.
Publishing results without consent. A profile is personal information, even if there’s nothing hurtful in it.
Treating a profile as permanent. A year later, in a new role, the result may shift, and that’s normal.

mbti.title: DISC vs MBTI vs Big Five: How They Differ and Which to Pick
mbti.description: DISC vs MBTI vs Big Five: what each model measures, how many types it has, how reliable it is, where it’s used and which test to choose. Free DISC test online.
mbti.h1: DISC vs MBTI: what’s the difference?
mbti.lead: DISC and MBTI are the two best-known typologies used with teams, and people mix them up all the time. Both give you four letters and both talk about “types,” but they measure different things and answer different questions. Below is a short comparison that also covers the Big Five, plus practical advice on which one to pick.

p: DISC describes observable behavior: how a person acts, communicates and makes decisions. It uses four scales: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness and Conscientiousness. The result is a primary and a secondary style, with 16 profiles in all. The model is simple on purpose and focused on work: what you need from colleagues and what they need from you.

MBTI (Myers–Briggs Type Indicator) sorts people into 16 types based on four dichotomies: extraversion vs. introversion, sensing vs. intuition, thinking vs. feeling and judging vs. perceiving. It’s a model of preferences in perception and decision-making, rooted in Jung’s typology. A type like INTJ or ESFP tells you how someone takes in information and what matters to them. It doesn’t tell you how they behave in a meeting.

The Big Five isn’t a typology but a set of five continuous traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. It’s the scientific standard in personality psychology, with the best reliability and predictive power, but a result made of five scales is harder to turn into practical advice.
The table simplifies things, but it makes the main point clear: DISC is about behavior, MBTI about preferences and the Big Five about traits.

sections.h: Can you convert MBTI to DISC?
p: There’s no exact match, because the models measure different things, but there are statistical links. In MBTI, extraversion tends to go with high D and I, and introversion with S and C. A preference for Thinking (T) leans toward D and C, and Feeling (F) toward I and S. So an ENTJ often gets a D or DC profile, an ESFP an I or IS, an ISFJ an S or SC, and an INTP a C or CD.

Treat this as a rough guide. People with the same MBTI type can get different DISC profiles depending on their role, and a DISC profile is more likely than an MBTI type to shift when someone changes jobs. If you want to know how a colleague will act in a specific situation, their DISC report tells you more than four MBTI letters.

MBTI is criticized for its artificial dichotomies: most people score near the middle of a scale, and a small change in answers puts them in a different type. DISC partly avoids this because it shows how strong each style is instead of placing you at one of two poles, but it’s still a self-report with moderate reliability. The Big Five is more reliable than both because it doesn’t try to sort people into types.

The practical takeaway: neither DISC nor MBTI should be the only basis for hiring or promotion decisions. Both work well as a language for talking about differences, and here DISC wins on simplicity. You can learn four styles in one meeting, but not 16 MBTI types.

ul: You want to improve communication on a team, assign roles or prepare for a negotiation: DISC. It deals with visible behavior and gives ready-made advice on how others can best communicate with you.
You want to understand yourself, where your preferences come from and where to grow: MBTI or the Big Five. They go deeper into inner attitudes.
You need data for research or a prediction, such as how dependable an employee will be: the Big Five. It has the strongest evidence base.
Not sure? Take DISC. It takes 10 minutes, it’s free, there’s no sign-up, and you can use the result at work right away.

p: Yes, and it’s worth it, because the models complement rather than contradict each other. MBTI will explain why you’re more comfortable working with ideas than with people, and DISC will show how that comes across to your colleagues and what to do about it. Save both results and compare them. The mismatches often turn out to be the most interesting part.

compatibility.title: DISC Compatibility Chart: How D, I, S and C Work Together
compatibility.description: DISC compatibility for every pair of styles: D–I, D–S, D–C, I–S, I–C, S–C and same-style pairs. What they share, where they clash and what helps. Free test.
compatibility.lead: No two DISC styles are incompatible: any pair can work well together once they understand how they differ. Still, every pair has its own strengths and its own typical conflicts. Pick two styles in the chart to see what they have in common, where friction comes from and what each person can do.

p: Here, compatibility doesn’t mean “are you right for each other.” It means how easily two styles understand each other without trying. Neighboring styles (D and I, I and S, S and C, C and D) share one axis, either pace or focus, and usually find common ground fast. Opposites (D and S, I and C) differ on both axes. They have the hardest time, but they also complement each other the most.

Matching styles get each other right away, but they also amplify the weaknesses they share: two Ds fight over the wheel, and two Ss can put off change for years. So an “easy” pair isn’t always a “strong” one, and a difficult pair that has agreed on ground rules gets the best results.

Start with each person’s primary style: yours from the test, the other person’s from the test or from what you’ve observed. Open the page for your pair and read both sets of tips, yours and theirs. It works best to go through the page together, with each of you picking one rule you’re willing to follow. If either of you has a strong secondary style, check that pair too. It will explain some of the behavior the primary style doesn’t.

DD.summary: Two people used to making the call and taking the lead. Together they move fast, but they compete for control and rarely back down.
DD.text: Two Ds bring speed and clarity. Both speak directly, neither minds directness in return, both decide quickly and neither can stand drawn-out discussions. Trouble starts when only one decision can win. Each is sure they’re right, both are used to winning, and an argument about the work easily turns into a fight over who’s in charge. To make the pair work, divide areas of responsibility up front.
common: Focus on results and deadlines
Straight talk without hints or hurt feelings
Willingness to take responsibility and risks
friction: A fight for control and the last word
Impatience: both interrupt and rush
Nobody checks the details or listens to the cautious

D: Agree on who owns what, and stay out of each other’s lane
Argue about what a good result looks like, not who’s right
Bring an S or a C into the discussion — they see what you both miss

deep.lead: A D manager and a D report agree fast on the essentials: the goal, the deadline, the result. Problems start when the report wants to make their own calls and the manager is used to making them for everyone. A clear boundary works best: the manager owns the “what” and the “by when,” and the report owns the “how.” If that line is blurry, every assignment turns into an argument about authority.
deep.meeting: In meetings, two Ds get down to business fast and start arguing just as fast. Both speak with confidence, interrupt and try to close the question with their own solution. In writing, they send short messages with no greeting. To outsiders it looks like a fight, but to them it’s just their normal tone. A facilitator is useful here: someone who records the decision and doesn’t let anyone reopen it.
deep.conflict: Their usual clash is over the last word. Both are sure their option is right, and neither will back down in public. What helps is agreeing on a criterion in advance (“we pick whatever brings in revenue faster”) and letting each of them save face. For this pair, an argument won in front of the team costs more than one lost in private.
deep.life: Outside work, two Ds make an energetic pair that’s never bored: shared goals, sports, competition, quick decisions. Their fights are loud and short. They need to divide responsibilities and keep every household question from turning into a duel.

Argue in private, not in front of the team
Agree on how you’ll choose before the argument, not during it

DI.summary: The most energetic pair: D sets the goal and the pace, I gets people fired up. Together they launch projects, but they tend to underestimate details and caution.
DI.text: D and I share a fast pace. Both decide on the fly, love a challenge and can’t stand routine. Where they differ is focus: D thinks about results, I about people and impressions. That makes them a good match. D brings direction and toughness; I brings contacts, morale and a knack for selling an idea. Friction starts when D sees I’s talkativeness as a waste of time and I finds D cold and abrupt. Both should remember that while they supply the energy, someone has to watch the details.

friction: D wants specifics, I gets carried away talking
I is hurt by bluntness, D is irritated by emotion
Both are too optimistic about deadlines and miss details

D: Open with a couple of minutes of personal talk, then get to business
Recognize I’s contribution out loud — it’s fuel for them
Don’t cut ideas off mid-flight: let them finish, then pick the best
I: Keep it short with a D: the result, the deadline, what you need from them
Put agreements in writing so enthusiasm doesn’t drift from the facts
Don’t take D’s directness personally — it’s a style, not a judgment

deep.lead: A D manager gives an I report a goal and expects results — and gets energy, connections and quick responses in return. But an I struggles with dry instructions and no recognition, so a D manager should praise out loud and hand out visible assignments. It’s better to check details and reports along the way than at the end.
deep.leadRev: An I manager gets a D report excited about an idea and gives them freedom, which the D appreciates. Friction starts when goals shift with every new idea, because inconsistency irritates a D. An I manager should pin down priorities and not change them without a reason. The D should raise disagreement one-on-one instead of arguing in front of the team.
deep.meeting: D and I are the loudest people in any meeting. D pushes for a decision, I for talking through ideas and people. Together they can sell an idea to everyone else fast. In writing, D is brief, while I writes with feeling and at length. D may find I’s messages empty; I may find D’s rude.
deep.conflict: A classic scenario: I promises a client more than the team can deliver on time, and D, the last to find out, blows up. Instead of asking “whose fault is it?”, set a rule: any promise about deadlines gets cleared with whoever is responsible for delivering. D should also remember that an I takes harshness in front of others as a betrayal.
deep.life: Off the clock, D and I are a lively, active pair: travel, groups of friends, new projects. Both love doing things and hate being bored. The risks are competing for attention and making impulsive decisions, so one of them should take charge of the budget and the calendar.
rules: Promise deadlines only after checking with whoever will deliver
Give recognition out loud: for an I it’s fuel, for a D a sign of respect
Put decisions in writing right after you talk

DS.summary: Opposites on both axes: D is fast and results-driven, S is measured and protects relationships. The hardest pair and one of the most useful.
DS.text: D and S differ in everything: pace, how they handle conflict, what they see as important. D sees S as slow and indecisive; S sees D as pushy and disrespectful. Yet they complement each other perfectly: D breaks ground and gets things started, while S holds steady, sees things through and keeps the team together. It only works with explicit rules. D eases off the pressure and gives advance notice of changes; S learns to say “no” and to voice disagreement out loud instead of going silent.
common: Practicality: both want the job done
Keeping commitments
A dislike of empty talk and posturing
friction: Pace: D rushes, S needs time
Conflict: D takes it on easily, S avoids it at all costs
S quietly agrees, then doesn’t follow through; D reads it as sabotage

D: Warn them about changes early and explain why
Ask for their view directly, then wait without filling the silence
Thank them for being reliable; an S won’t ask for recognition
S: Voice disagreement right away, briefly and to the point — a D respects that
Ask for clear deadlines and priorities instead of guessing
Don’t take D’s drive as hostility; it’s just their normal speed

deep.lead: A D manager with an S report is the most common pairing and the most fragile. D assigns tasks fast and changes them on the fly; S tries to get it all done and quietly gets overloaded. A D manager should give advance notice of changes and ask “what’s getting in your way?” instead of “why isn’t it done?” Then the S becomes the most reliable person on that manager’s team.
deep.leadRev: An S manager gives a D report a calm, predictable environment, but the D may get bored there and start going over the manager’s head. An S manager should give the D a measurable goal and freedom. The D, in turn, shouldn’t mistake the manager’s gentleness for weakness and should share their next steps in advance.
deep.meeting: At the meeting table, D speaks first and at length; S speaks last or not at all. If D doesn’t ask S directly, the team loses its most clear-eyed read on the risks. In writing, D expects an instant reply, while S answers later, after thinking it over. D reads the pause as sabotage; S reads the pressure as rudeness.
deep.conflict: It usually goes like this: D announces urgent changes, and S agrees but keeps doing things the old way. D gets angry, S feels hurt. To break the pattern, give S time to ask “how will this affect what I’m working on now?” and agree on what to drop to make room for the new task. D gets speed, and S gets clarity.
deep.life: In everyday life, D and S often complement each other: one proposes and decides, the other builds a home and stability. The danger is that S gives in for years and quietly builds up resentment while D doesn’t notice. This pair needs regular, calm conversations about what matters to each of them.
rules: Announce changes in advance and explain them
Ask S’s opinion separately and wait for the answer
S says “no” in words, not with silence

DC.summary: Both focus on the task and the result, but D wants it fast and C wants it right. A strong pair for complex projects once they agree on pace.
DC.text: D and C share a focus on the task. For both, the work matters more than the atmosphere; both value competence and don’t waste time on small talk. The difference is pace: D decides with half the data, while C wants to gather everything and check it. D sees C as a brake who plays it too safe; C sees D as irresponsible. On a complex project this is the best combination: D keeps things moving, and C delivers quality and guards against mistakes. The key is to decide up front where you need speed and where you need precision.
common: Focus on the task and the result, not on relationships
Respect for competence and logic
Directness: both prefer facts to emotions
friction: D decides fast, C wants data and time
C reads drive as pressure, D reads caution as sabotage
Both are critical and stingy with recognition

D: Give C time to analyze, and say up front when you need an answer
Back your decisions with facts, not “because I said so”
Split the work: where mistakes are costly, C gets the last word
C: Offer D a “good enough for now” option instead of “perfect later”
Flag risks briefly, with the likely consequences, and skip the long justification
Don’t wait for praise from a D — to them, no criticism is approval

deep.lead: A D manager expects fast results from a C report, while the C expects clear criteria and time to do quality work. If D rushes them without explaining why, C slows down even more. What works is an agreement: D names the deadline and the acceptable level of quality, and C flags risks right away. Then D gets results without surprises, and C gets the chance to do it right.
deep.leadRev: A C manager builds processes and standards, while a D report races toward results and works around the rules. A C manager should explain which rules are mandatory and why, and give the D freedom on everything else. The D, for their part, gets further by coming to the C with numbers instead of pressure.
deep.meeting: When they meet, D wants to decide now and C wants to understand first. D calls C’s questions nitpicking; C thinks D’s decisions are rushed. A “decision + review date” format helps: make the call today and look at the data in a week. In writing, both are brief and to the point, so it’s easier for them than meetings.
deep.conflict: The typical conflict: D sends a client a solution C hasn’t checked yet, and the mistake surfaces on the client’s end. C says “I warned you,” D says “we had to move faster.” The fix is to agree in advance on what never goes out without C’s check and what can go out right away.
deep.life: In personal relationships, D and C are two strong personalities focused on tasks more than feelings. They respect each other’s competence but can forget about warmth. Their plans together are well thought out, and disagreements go better when they’re settled with facts instead of pressure.
rules: Agree on speed and quality before the work starts
Argue with facts, not pressure or rule-quoting
Spell out what never goes out unchecked

II.summary: Two people who love people, ideas and attention. They have fun together and things come easily, but someone has to watch the deadlines and details.
II.text: Two Is bring energy, optimism and a stream of ideas. They click fast, back each other up and create the kind of atmosphere people want to work in. The trouble comes from outside: promises made, deadlines forgotten, details nobody checked. Another trap is competing for attention. Both want the spotlight, and the conversation turns into two monologues. This pair needs an outside anchor: written action items, a calendar and a high-C or high-S colleague.
common: Sociability and easy rapport
Optimism and faith in ideas
A dislike of formalities and routine
friction: Both talk, nobody listens
Promises without a plan: deadlines and details slip
Conflicts get smoothed over to keep the peace

I: End every meeting with a list: who, what, by when
Split the roles: one runs the conversation, the other takes notes
Ask a C or an S to check the plan before you announce it

deep.lead: An I manager and an I report are on the same wavelength: lots of ideas, praise and lively conversation. The trouble is follow-through. The manager forgets what they assigned, and the report forgets what they promised. They need structure from outside: tasks in writing, a shared calendar and a short, regular check-in on deadlines.
deep.meeting: Put two Is in a meeting and any discussion becomes a brainstorm: interesting and fun, but with no outcome. Both want to talk, and neither listens very well. A set agenda keeps them on track: time for ideas, then who does what. In writing there’s plenty of emotion, emojis and voice messages, and important agreements get lost among them.
deep.conflict: Most of their conflicts come down to unspoken resentment. Both avoid an unpleasant conversation to keep the mood good, until the problem grows. They should agree to raise problems right away and in private, and to keep criticism of the work separate from how they feel about the person.
deep.life: Away from work, two Is are the life of the party: friends, celebrations, trips. Being together comes easily, but chores, money and plans often go unattended. They should divide up the boring tasks explicitly, or nobody will do them.
rules: Every meeting ends with a list: who, what, when
Say unpleasant things right away and in private
Get a C or an S to check the plan before announcing it

IS.summary: A warm, friendly pair: I inspires, S supports. Good for the atmosphere and for clients, less so for hard decisions.
IS.text: I and S share a focus on people: relationships, atmosphere and recognition matter to both. The difference is pace. I is fast, spontaneous and loves new things; S is measured and prefers the familiar routine. Together they create the friendliest environment on the team, but they struggle with tough decisions, avoid unpleasant conversations and can let a problem drag on just so nobody gets hurt. I can nudge S toward change, and S can keep I from making impulsive promises.
common: Attention to people and relationships
A wish for harmony and a good atmosphere
Readiness to help and support
friction: I changes plans on the fly, which throws S off
Both avoid conflict, and problems pile up
I talks a lot, S gives in and keeps quiet about their needs

I: Warn S about changes early, and don’t reverse decisions without a reason
Ask for S’s opinion directly, since they won’t volunteer it
Finish what you start — S values reliability above ideas
S: Say your boundaries out loud; an I won’t guess them
Support I’s ideas, but ask for a plan and deadlines
Don’t be afraid of honest feedback — an I will take it better than you think

deep.lead: An I manager inspires and praises, and an S report delivers reliably. It’s a good pairing as long as the I doesn’t change plans every week. Constant change is hard on an S, and they won’t say so on their own. An I manager should ask how the S is coping and keep priorities steady.
deep.leadRev: An S manager creates a calm atmosphere where an I report feels comfortable, but may not give them enough recognition and visibility. An S manager should acknowledge the I’s wins out loud; the I should remember that an S values consistency and dislikes surprises.
deep.meeting: In meetings, I talks while S listens and backs them up. The meeting goes pleasantly, but contentious issues often get sidestepped because neither likes conflict. In writing, I is fast and prolific, while S is careful and slower to reply. I may conclude that S isn’t interested.
deep.conflict: Here’s how it often goes: I changes the plan at the last minute, and S quietly adjusts but loses trust. The two should agree that changes get discussed in advance and that S says out loud when something doesn’t work for them. Both need to learn to disagree without worrying it will hurt the relationship.
deep.life: Outside work, I and S are a warm, friendly pair with lots of conversation and care. I brings new experiences; S brings comfort and stability. The risk is that hard conversations get put off for years. Now and then, the two should deliberately set aside time to talk about what isn’t working.
rules: Discuss changes in advance, not after the fact
S voices discomfort in words
Don’t be afraid to disagree: it won’t break the relationship

IC.summary: Opposites: I thrives on people and impressions, C on facts and precision. A difficult pair that turns into a strong one once trust is there.
IC.text: I and C differ on both axes, pace and focus. I talks a lot, decides fast and goes by feel; C talks little, decides after checking and goes by the data. To C, I seems shallow; to I, C seems tedious and cold. Yet together they cover each other’s blind spots: I sells, inspires and negotiates, and C makes sure what was promised actually works. It takes mutual respect: I values the checking, and C values the personal contact.
common: An interest in ideas, though from different angles
A desire to do things well: I beautifully, C correctly
No power struggle: neither needs control for its own sake
friction: I promises, C checks and finds gaps
C needs quiet and time, I needs interaction and speed
I’s emotions irritate C, C’s reserve hurts I

I: Prepare facts and figures before talking to a C
Give a C time to answer — silence means thinking, not refusing
Don’t take criticism of the details as rejection of the idea
C: Start by acknowledging the idea, then move on to the risks
Explain your conclusions in plain language, without listing all the data
Sometimes settle for “good enough” — not every detail is worth an argument

deep.lead: An I manager gives tasks in broad, emotional terms, while a C report expects a precise brief. If I doesn’t spell out the criteria, C will keep asking follow-up questions or do the wrong thing. An I manager should assign tasks in writing, with examples and deadlines; the C should ask questions right away, not afterward.
deep.leadRev: A C manager gives an I report detailed instructions and checks the details, while the I wants freedom and recognition. A C manager should open feedback with what went well and leave the I room to work with people. The I, in turn, gets further by sending the C facts, not just impressions.
deep.meeting: I brings ideas to the meeting, and C looks for weak spots in them. I takes C’s questions as rejection; C finds I’s enthusiasm shallow. Separating the stages works well: ideas first with no criticism, then the analysis. In writing, I is emotional and C is structured, so each should adapt to the other’s format.
deep.conflict: A typical flare-up: I shows a client numbers C hasn’t checked yet, and one of them turns out to be wrong. C is annoyed, and I is stung by a public mistake. A simple rule prevents this: numbers for outside presentations go through C, and C turns them around quickly.
deep.life: In their personal lives, I and C are opposites: I is drawn to people and spontaneity, C to plans and quiet. They can be a very balanced pair if I respects C’s need for space and C doesn’t dampen I’s enthusiasm with criticism.
rules: Ideas first, criticism second — as separate stages
C checks any numbers that go outside
Start criticism with what went well

SS.summary: The calmest pair: reliability, patience and mutual support. The danger is getting stuck and avoiding difficult topics.
SS.text: Two Ss understand each other without words. Both value stability, keep their promises, listen and don’t push. This pair can work steadily and without conflict for years. The flip side is avoiding anything that disturbs the peace: change, arguments, unpleasant conversations. Problems get endured rather than solved, and decisions get postponed because nobody wants to take the first step. They benefit from an outside push: firm deadlines, a high-D manager or a high-I colleague who will shake things up.
common: Reliability and consistency
Patience and the ability to listen
Loyalty to the team and to familiar ways of working
friction: Nobody starts change or takes the initiative
Disagreements get buried, resentment builds
Decisions stall while each waits for someone else to decide

S: Set deadlines for each other; without them, nothing moves
Agree to name problems out loud, even small ones
Take turns being “the one who decides”

deep.lead: An S manager and an S report make for calm, reliable work without conflict. The weak spot is change and tough decisions, since both put them off. An S manager should set deadlines for decisions and prepare the team for change in advance; the report should raise problems without waiting to be asked.
deep.meeting: Meetings between two Ss are polite, attentive and quiet. Decisions come slowly, and sensitive topics stay off the table. A team with this pair feels calm, but it can miss the moment for change. A clear deadline helps: “we’ll decide by Friday.”
deep.conflict: Their conflict is usually invisible: both are unhappy but stay silent, and tension builds for months. The remedy is short, regular one-on-ones built around the question “what’s getting in your way?” and an agreement that disagreement is normal.
deep.life: Outside work, two Ss are a reliable, cozy pair who value traditions, home and constancy. They rarely feel cramped together. The risk is getting stuck: both put off change, even when it’s needed. From time to time, they should deliberately try something new together.
rules: Set deadlines for decisions instead of waiting forever
Disagreement is normal; say it out loud
Plan changes in small steps

SC.summary: A measured, thorough pair: S looks after relationships, C looks after quality. Excellent for support work and processes, hard on change.
SC.text: S and C share a measured pace. Neither likes to rush; both value order and predictability and think their steps through. The difference is focus: S thinks about people and harmony, C about rules and facts. Together they build the most stable processes on the team, but they have a hard time accepting anything new, and when change comes, they go through it together, slowly. Their typical conflict is a quiet one: C criticizes mistakes and seems callous to S, while S bends the rules for people’s sake and seems lax to C.
common: Caution and careful decisions
Respect for order and commitments
An aversion to haste, chaos and pressure
friction: C puts rules above relationships, S does the opposite
Both resist change, and the team stands still
S takes C’s criticism as personal coldness

S: Read C’s critiques as care for quality, not a verdict on you
Ask them to explain the logic of a rule instead of arguing with the rule
Suggest changes in small steps — easier for you and for C
C: Soften criticism: what’s good first, then what to fix
Remember that for an S, the atmosphere is part of the result
Recognize S’s contribution out loud; they won’t ask for it

deep.lead: An S manager and a C report make a calm, careful pairing. S values C’s reliability; C values S’s predictability. The risks are slow decisions and avoiding conflict, so issues that call for a firm hand get put off. An S manager should set deadlines and give the C clear criteria.
deep.leadRev: A C manager gives an S report clear rules and processes, and the S feels confident working within them. But the C can be too critical and cold, and the S may quietly take offense. A C manager should acknowledge the S’s reliability out loud; the S should ask about the criteria up front.
deep.meeting: In meetings, S and C take their time: they go through questions in detail and weigh decisions carefully. Meetings can drag on, and the outcome can get fuzzy. In writing, both are careful and polite. The main thing is not to sit on questions that need a decision.
deep.conflict: The typical conflict: C critiques S’s work point by point, and S takes it in silence and loses motivation. C can head this off by starting with what was done well and explaining the criteria in advance; S, by speaking up when the criticism seems unfair.
deep.life: Outside work, S and C are a calm, thoughtful pair: plans, order, attention to detail. They’re comfortable together but short on spontaneity. Breaking out of their usual routine now and then does them good.
rules: Explain the criteria before the work, not after
The good first, then the critique
Set deadlines for your decisions

CC.summary: A pair of experts: precision, logic and high standards. Together they do flawless work, but slowly, and they tend to argue over small things.
CC.text: Two Cs speak the same language: facts, criteria, risks. They respect each other’s expertise and turn out work no one can fault. The problem is pace and perfectionism. Every detail gets discussed, every decision waits for complete certainty, and an argument over a comma can drag on for a week. Another trap is reserve: neither talks about tension, and disagreements turn into cold silence. This pair needs an outside deadline and a shared understanding that “good enough” is fine too.
common: High quality standards
Reliance on data and logic
Discipline and keeping commitments
friction: Perfectionism doubles and deadlines slip
Arguments over details with no decision on the substance
Tension goes unspoken and builds up

C: Decide in advance what quality level is good enough, and stop there
Limit analysis time — a decision on time beats a perfect one with no deadline
Talk about disagreements directly; silence doesn’t solve anything

deep.lead: A C manager and a C report understand each other without many words: standards, data, precision. The hard parts are speed and criticism, since both tend to double-check and find flaws. A C manager should define what “good enough” means and point out successes, not just mistakes.
deep.meeting: When two Cs meet, they go through the issue in detail, ask precise questions and rarely reach a quick decision. Their meetings are high quality but long. In writing, they send detailed emails with attachments. They do better opening with the conclusion than with the analysis.
deep.conflict: Most often they clash over method. Both are sure their way is right and can keep making the case forever. The way out is to agree on how to judge the options and on a deadline after which the decision gets made, even without complete certainty.
deep.life: At home and with friends, two Cs are a calm, considered pair who value personal space, order and honesty. They rarely fight loudly but can be too critical of each other. They should talk more often about what makes them happy, not only about what’s wrong.
rules: Define “good enough” in advance
Open emails and conversations with the conclusion
Point out successes, not just mistakes

howMade.title: How AI Prepares DISC Reports — Automatically, Without Bias
howMade.description: How DISC reports are made: AI wrote the texts in advance under our editorial rules, and a program builds your report from your answers with no human involved.
howMade.lead: Both the summary and in-depth reports on this site are prepared automatically. Artificial intelligence wrote the texts, following rules set by our editorial team, and a program assembles your report from your answers with no human involved. So your report isn’t colored by anyone’s first impressions, mood or expectations.
howMade.stepsTitle: From answers to report in three steps
steps: You answer. The test has 24 blocks. In each one, you mark the statement that’s most like you and the one that’s least like you. Only these answers go into the calculation.

The program does the scoring. For each of the four styles, it subtracts your “least” marks from your “most” marks. Those numbers determine your profile, one of 16. The formula is public, and the “{results}” page walks you through it.

The program builds the report. From a set of texts AI wrote in advance, it picks the ones that fit your profile and your numbers. The summary report appears on screen right away. The in-depth report is assembled after you pay and sent to you by email.

p: The report texts were written by a large language model, a type of artificial intelligence that works with text. For the summary report, it wrote descriptions of the four styles and the 16 profiles. For the in-depth report, it wrote 13 sections for each profile, including how others see you, your strengths, growth areas, communicating with each of the four styles, conflict and stress, and a 30-day plan.

For the in-depth report, it also wrote separate texts tied to your numbers: what each of the four scales means at each of five levels, from very low to very high, and what to do about your lowest scale. Only the texts that match your answers go into your report.
The AI wrote the texts in advance, not when you place your order. We did this on purpose, so the text can be checked before it reaches you and the same answers always produce the same report.
The program calculates your result and assembles the report. For the summary report, that means your profile, the chart, your percentages on the four scales and your profile description.

In the in-depth report, the entire section on your profile depends on your numbers: your percentages, a close look at each scale and a comparison of the two layers of your answers. In five other sections, certain passages are chosen based on your lowest scale. The rest of the text is written for your profile, and your name is on every page.
The program doesn’t make anything up as it goes. Only what follows from your answers ends up in the report.
Our editorial team set the rules the AI wrote by. The main ones:
ul: Reports describe tendencies, not abilities or destiny. No diagnoses, no promises.
All styles are equal: none is described as better or worse than another.
The in-depth report includes no numbers or sweeping claims that data doesn’t back up, and every piece of advice is something you can do this week: a ready-made phrase, a rule, a deadline.
The in-depth report makes no assumptions about your gender: the program doesn’t know who you are, and the text doesn’t try to guess.
after: Our editorial team read the in-depth report template for each of the 16 profiles before it went on sale. Your own report isn’t prepared by a person, and no one reads it before it goes out. A program assembles and sends it.
If you spot a mistake or something inaccurate, let us know through the “{contact}” form.

benefits.p: Your report is built from your answers and nothing else. We ask for your name only to put it on the pages. The program doesn’t know your gender, age, job title or what you look like. It has no first impressions and no favorite or least favorite types.
The same answers always produce the same report. A person’s conclusions can depend on experience, fatigue and mood. The program’s depend only on your answers.

The summary report appears on screen as soon as you finish the last block. The in-depth report is assembled at any hour, day or night, with no appointment and no waiting list, and the email with your report arrives right after payment.
Because the reports are prepared automatically, we can keep the test and the summary report free and offer the in-depth report for US${price}.

benefits.h: Your answers don’t go to an AI
benefits.p: No one has to read your answers to prepare your report, because a program processes them. Since the texts are written in advance, your answers, name and email address aren’t shared with third-party AI services. The “{privacy}” page describes what data the site stores.
All 16 profiles follow the same structure and get the same level of detail. AI doesn’t get tired toward the end of a text, and it doesn’t write less about a rare profile than a common one.
The report isn’t trying to win you over. It’s as direct about your weaknesses as about your strengths, and it doesn’t sort styles into good and bad.
The numbers in the report match the ones on your result screen, and the scoring method is described openly. You can retake the test and compare results.

limits: It doesn’t know your life. It draws on your test answers and the typical picture of your profile. Your circumstances, experience and values aren’t part of it. Some of it you’ll recognize right away, and some won’t sound like you.
It doesn’t correct your answers. The test is a self-report: if you answer the way you think you should rather than the way things are, the report will describe the person you’d like to be.
It doesn’t diagnose anything or assess abilities. The report doesn’t replace a psychologist and shouldn’t be the sole basis for hiring or other personnel decisions.
It isn’t error-proof. We read and edit the texts the AI wrote, but mistakes can still slip through. If you spot one, let us know.

faq.q: Are my answers sent to an AI?
faq.a: No. The AI wrote the texts in advance and never sees your answers. An ordinary program, running in your browser and on the site’s server, calculates your result and assembles your report. Your answers aren’t shared with third-party AI services.

faq.q: Does the AI write the report for me personally?
faq.a: The report is assembled for you personally, but it isn’t written from scratch. The text is written for your profile, one of 16, and the sections with numbers and certain passages are chosen to match your answers. That’s why the report can be checked and doesn’t depend on chance.

faq.q: Does anyone read my report before it’s sent?
faq.a: No. Our editorial team read the report templates ahead of time. Your own report is assembled and sent automatically.

faq.q: Can the AI get things wrong?
faq.a: Yes, just as a person can. That’s why a formula calculates the numbers instead of AI, the texts were written to a set of rules, and our editorial team read them. If anything in your report seems inaccurate, let us know. We’ll check it and fix it.

faq.q: How is a report like this different from a session with a consultant?
faq.a: A consultant talks through your particular situation with you and can ask follow-up questions. The report can’t do that. It describes your style based on your test answers. Still, it’s handy to bring along, whether you’re seeing a consultant or talking with your manager.

p: The site is run by the disc-test.org editorial team: we write the copy, maintain the code and answer email. The project is independent. The test and the result are free, with no sign-up and no third-party ads. Our only paid service is the in-depth DISC profile (see “Services”). We don’t sell training or certifications, and we aren’t affiliated with Wiley (DiSC®), TTI Success Insights or any other trademark holder.

We’re responsible for everything published on the site. If you spot an error in the text, an inaccurate translation or a mismatch between how we describe the method and how the score is actually calculated, write to us. We’ll fix it and update the “last updated” date.

sections.h: How we write and check our content
p: Our claims about the method rest on primary sources and peer-reviewed research, including critical studies; you’ll find the list in the “{sources}” section. We don’t paraphrase commercial reports. Our editorial team prepared the descriptions of the four styles and the 16 profiles with AI assistance, based on the model’s generally accepted characteristics.

Every page shows the date it was last updated. We revise our content when the test itself changes or when readers point something out, and we don’t publish anything we can’t back up with a source or our own checks.

get: Your primary and secondary style and your profile name — one of 16
A three-line chart showing how strong each style is, in percent
Your strengths, growth areas, motivation and behavior under stress
Tips on how best to communicate and work with you
A link to your report and a PDF copy — no sign-up and no paid versions
home.calc: In each of the 24 blocks, you mark one statement as most like you and one as least like you. Each statement belongs to one of the styles: D, I, S or C. A style’s score is its “most” marks minus its “least” marks, from −24 to +24, and it’s then converted to a percentage. The style with the highest score is your primary style. A secondary style counts if it also clearly stands out.

faq.q: How long does it take?
faq.a: About 10 minutes: 24 blocks of four statements each.

faq.q: Is it free?
faq.a: Yes. The test and the result are free, with no sign-up and no third-party ads. Only the in-depth DISC profile is paid, and it’s optional.

faq.q: Are there right answers?
faq.a: No. Every profile is normal. Answer the way you usually act at work, not the way you’d like to.

faq.q: Can a whole team take the test?
faq.a: Yes. Everyone takes the test from a link, and the results are collected in the admin panel.

p: For each style, the test subtracts your “least like me” answers from your “most like me” answers, for a total from −24 to +24. The style with the highest total becomes your primary style and the first letter of your profile. The second-highest style counts as secondary if its total is positive, at least 40% of the primary one and no less than 3 points; it then becomes the second letter.

If the second style falls short of that bar, the profile is pure: D, I, S or C. If it clears the bar, you get one of 12 combinations. Four pure profiles plus 12 combinations make up the 16 profiles in the table above.

A style is one of the four DISC scales: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness or Conscientiousness. A profile describes how the styles combine in a particular person: the primary style sets the core of their behavior, and the secondary style adds a shade. That’s why DI and ID share the same letters but are different profiles. The Pioneer (DI) goes for results first and brings people along the way. The Motivator (ID) gets people on board first and reaches results through them.
A profile isn’t a label or a grade. Everyone has all four styles; the profile simply shows which ones come through most strongly in a familiar work setting.

Take the free test: 24 blocks of four statements, about 10 minutes. Your result screen shows a chart, your primary and secondary style and a link to your profile page, which covers compatibility with other styles and tips on how you work and communicate best.

ui.print.countText: For each style, count the number of “most like me” marks and the number of “least like me” marks, then subtract the second from the first. The total ranges from −24 to +24, and the totals of the four styles add up to zero.
ui.print.decodeText: The primary style is the one with the highest total. If the second-highest total is positive and at least 40% of the primary one (minimum 3 points), it is the secondary style. A profile is written as one letter (for example, D) or two (for example, DI: primary D, secondary I). If no total is above 2, the profile is balanced: the styles are expressed about equally.
